synopsis: Heavy off-road stopping depends on ground conditions as much as brakes, with grade, payload, tyre or track condition, brake temperature, hydraulic response and articulation changing stopping distance and the safe intervention point [f11374, f7452, f5818]. Transfer from road AEB remains unresolved: dry-asphalt assumptions and road-oriented standards do not establish validity for deformable surfaces or heavy machinery, and published validation of simulated heavy-machine braking distance on gravel, mud, ice or slopes was not found [f2571, f7696, f11349, f253, f3970]. The 2019 Jimblebar collision involved an unloaded autonomous truck losing traction in bad weather; unintended full braking can also be hazardous, and Komatsu documentation accessed in 2026 advises disabling loader stop control on steep slopes and slippery or soft ground [f1375, f2342, f10550]. Queensland guidance requires stopping assumptions to cover worst relevant combinations of wet or slippery roads, downhill grade, maximum speed, full load, poor tyres and brake delay, rather than a single proving-ground surface [f3403, f2901]. The recommended validation approach retains physical stopping tests across machine, load, slope and surface extremes, bounds dynamics models with those results, and reserves high-fidelity soil simulation for traction-sensitive cases; a proposed stopping-distance matrix covers two machine families across three surfaces and grades [f7881, f10612, f9325, f10940].
